clue.text: Cuban's heedlessly concealing wailing spirit

indicators.note: to conceal is to keep something tucked inside, so the answer lies within the run of words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A careless Cuban is somehow hiding a howling ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored: the letters run from inside 'Cuban's' into 'heedlessly' to give BANSHEE.
explanation.definitionFit: In Irish folklore this female spirit keens loudly outside a house to foretell a death there.

clue.text: Farewell purchase for the audience

indicators.note: an audience listens rather than reads, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: to purchase is to buy, which is spoken identically

explanation.surface: A parting gift bought to please the crowd at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' is a verb here: to buy, which is pronounced like the parting word.
explanation.definitionFit: A short casual word people say when leaving, a clipped form of goodbye.

clue.text: No gambling and drinking, say, for beginners

parts.note: taken as written
gambling and drinking are examples of bad habits

explanation.surface: A house rule for newcomers: no betting and no booze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks gambling and drinking as examples of a wider class, here vices.
explanation.definitionFit: Novices are people new to an activity, learners who are just starting out.

clue.text: Religious adherent back with uniform

parts.note: hind means rear, as in hind legs
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A believer returns to the faith wearing uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a reversal signal but simply means hind.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Hinduism, the major religion of India, is one example of a believer.

clue.text: Volume of rabble-rousing cut at first

indicators.note: cutting at the start removes the opening letter

parts.note: stirring up the mob against the state

explanation.surface: The noise level of a riot was turned down from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' reads as loudness, which suits rabble-rousing, but it means a book. Losing the S from SEDITION leaves EDITION.
explanation.definitionFit: A particular printing or issue of a book can be called a volume or an edition.

clue.text: Art gallery in North Dakota, say, not South

indicators.note: 'not' means leave out, and South abbreviates to a single letter

parts.note: North Dakota is an example of a US state

explanation.surface: A picture gallery found in the American Midwest.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the standard abbreviation for South. The TATE is a group of national art galleries in Britain, chiefly in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tate galleries, such as Tate Modern, house the British national collection of modern and historic art.

clue.text: Subject to incomplete selection

indicators.note: something incomplete is missing a part, here its last letter

parts.note: taken as written
a choice is a pick

explanation.surface: Something liable to a partial choosing, like a sample.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject to' reads as one phrase meaning liable to; split it, and 'to' becomes wordplay. PICK loses its K.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the matter being discussed or written about, the theme of a talk.

clue.text: Squire out to change order for precious stone

indicators.note: changing the order of letters rearranges them into a new word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A country gentleman sets out to reorganise things to get a gem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like part of the anagram signal but is fodder; 'to change order' does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Turquoise is a blue-green mineral cut and polished as a semi-precious gem for jewellery.

clue.text: Fling with head of navy is paradise

parts.note: to fling is to throw, or heave

indicators.note: the head of something is its top or front, its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of navy

explanation.surface: A romantic fling with a naval commander is bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' suggests a brief affair, but here it is a verb: to throw hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven and paradise are both names for the blissful abode of the blessed after death.

clue.text: Give naughty child paintings, perhaps

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
paintings are an example of art

explanation.surface: A request to hand a badly behaved youngster some pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' reads as an instruction to the solver but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to grant or bestow something, such as knowledge or a quality, on someone.

clue.text: Old lady and two friends cropped arresting picture showing ancient site

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold, so one part grips another
cropping trims the end off something, removing a final letter

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
a friend is a chum, and there are two of them
pic is short for picture

explanation.surface: Mum and a couple of mates hold a striking photo of a ruined city.
explanation.walkthrough: Each CHUM loses its M, and the pair of CHUs hold PIC between them. 'Old lady' is crossword shorthand for a mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Machu Picchu is a fifteenth-century Inca citadel high in the Andes of Peru, now a famous ruin.

clue.text: Italian family ultimately ban nausea pill having therapeutic properties

parts.note: the Medici were the ruling banking family of Renaissance Florence

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so each word gives its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: An Italian clan finally prohibits a travel-sickness tablet with healing effects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' applies to all three following words, not only 'ban'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something medicinal can treat or cure illness, the quality of a remedy or drug.

clue.text: Team returns, working for inventor

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a team is a side
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A squad gets back to work on behalf of a creator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' looks like the team coming home; it reverses SIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison was the American who patented the phonograph and a practical electric light bulb.

clue.text: Redesign phone or one has no chance of succeeding?

definitions.text: one has no chance of succeeding

indicators.note: to redesign is to rework the layout, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sceptic's question: rebuild the phone, or is it a lost cause?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a conjunction in the surface but is part of the fodder; the definition reads 'one [who] has no chance'.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-hoper is a person or entrant thought certain to fail, an outsider without prospects.

clue.text: Sleep next to family's serviette

indicators.note: being next to something means sitting beside it, so the parts join side by side

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: Dozing off beside the family's dinner napkin.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Serviette is the chiefly British word for the cloth or paper square used at meals to wipe hands and lips.

clue.text: Stapler is unusual first aid item!

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the normal order, so these letters take a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd thing to find in a medical kit: an office stapler.
explanation.walkthrough: A plaster, in British English, is an adhesive bandage (a Band-Aid).
explanation.definitionFit: A sticking plaster is a small adhesive dressing for covering cuts, standard in any medical kit.

clue.text: Desirable partner reportedly unravels slogan

parts.note: a good catch is someone highly eligible for marriage

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is taken by sound

parts.note: to unravel at the edges is to fray

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that an eligible match is coming apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unravels' is a verb, frays, which sounds exactly like the noun PHRASE.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchphrase is a well-known repeated saying, used like a motto or advertising line.

clue.text: Where one can find core temperature approximately

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
'or so' means roughly, as in ten or so

explanation.surface: A question about where to measure body heat roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Core temperature' looks like one phrase, but the split falls between them: the core is the definition's muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk of the body, between neck and hips, contains the abdominal and back muscles trainers call the core.

clue.text: Nun's garment beginning to harden slightly

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of harden
'a bit' means slightly, as in a bit tired

explanation.surface: A nun's robe starting to stiffen a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to' looks like part of the verb phrase 'beginning to harden', but it selects the first letter only.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is the long loose robe worn by members of a religious order of sisters.

clue.text: Catch Eminem song about otorhinolaryngology?

parts.note: the medical speciality of ear, nose and throat, abbreviated ENT
Eminem is a rapper, so his songs are rap

explanation.surface: An absurd idea: a rap track by Eminem on the subject of ear, nose and throat medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' means concerning: an ENT rap is a rap about that subject, so the subject comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrap is to snare or capture someone, often by trickery, which is to catch them.

clue.text: Outlaw grabs cash machine for superhero

indicators.note: to grab something is to hold it, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: to outlaw something is to ban it
ATM is an automated teller machine

explanation.surface: A bandit robs an ATM, a job for the caped crusader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' looks like a noun for the criminal but works as the verb ban.
explanation.definitionFit: Batman is the DC Comics crime-fighter of Gotham City, one of the best-known costumed heroes.

clue.text: Help Matilda regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Someone helps Matilda on a routine basis.
explanation.walkthrough: Start from the second letter of Matilda and take every other one.
explanation.definitionFit: To aid someone is to assist or support them; as nouns, aid and help are synonyms too.

clue.text: Singer heading east within Scotland

indicators.note: the answer reads eastward in the grid, the opposite way to the letters in the word
within means inside, so the answer sits inside the word

parts.note: the middle letters of the word

explanation.surface: A vocalist travelling eastward through Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: OTLA sits inside ScOTLAnd; written backwards it gives ALTO.
explanation.definitionFit: An alto is a singer with a low female or high male voice, between soprano and tenor.

clue.text: Engineers tried out not working any more

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Engineers tested things that have stopped functioning.
explanation.walkthrough: RE for engineers is a crossword staple from the Royal Engineers. 'Out' looks like part of 'tried out', meaning tested, but it shuffles TRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone retired has left their job for good, usually at pension age, and no longer works.
